modules.name: Money Master
modules.description: Identify and count different denominations and calculate totals.

lessons.title: Know Your Coins & Notes
lessons.content: Money comes in coins and notes, and each one carries a value you can read from the number printed on it. Pennies, nickels, dimes, and quarters are coins; notes come in $1, $5, $10, $20, $50, and $100.

interactive_section.question: How much is a coin marked "25" worth?
Which note is worth the most: $5, $20, or $100?

lessons.title: Counting Total Value
lessons.content: To find a total, group matching coins and notes, then add them. Start with the largest values first — it keeps the adding simple and fast.

interactive_section.question: Two quarters and three dimes equal how many cents?
A $20 note, a $10 note, and a $5 note total how much?

lessons.title: The Quick Total
lessons.content: Practice adding a mixed handful: count the notes first, then the coins, then combine the two.

interactive_section.question: A $1 note, three quarters, and a nickel add up to how much?

labs.name: Count & Conquer
labs.description: Sort a messy money tray and total every denomination quickly.
labs.intro: You are running the money table at the school fair. Coins and notes are all mixed up — sort them, count them, and make change for happy customers.

steps.task: Sort the tray by putting each coin with its matching value group. Which order works best?
The fair booth earned two $5 notes, three $1 notes, and a quarter. What is the total?
You buy a lemonade for 95¢ and pay with a $1 note and a nickel. How much change do you get?

modules.name: Make the Change
modules.description: Run a simulated shop and give customers the correct change.

lessons.title: Change Is a Difference
lessons.content: Change is what you get back when you pay more than a price. Work it out as: amount paid − price.

interactive_section.question: You pay $5 for a $3 toy. How much change do you get?
The price is $1.25 and you pay $2. How much change?

lessons.title: Counting Back, Up and Up
lessons.content: Count the change UP from the price to the amount paid. Starting low and climbing to the paid amount is the fastest way to stay correct.

interactive_section.question: From 35¢ up to $1, which coins do you count back first?
interactive_section.answer: A quarter, then two dimes, then a nickel

interactive_section.question: From $4.50 up to $5, what do you hand back?

lessons.title: Hand-Over & Smile
lessons.content: Give change using the fewest coins and notes when you can. Your customers will thank you — and your till will stay neater too.

interactive_section.question: What is 30¢ of change using the fewest coins?
What is $3 of change using the fewest notes?

labs.name: Penny Pals Shop
labs.description: Run the corner shop register and give every customer the correct change.
labs.intro: Welcome to your own shop counter! Customers will hand you cash — count the change carefully so everyone walks away happy.

steps.task: A pencil costs 30¢. The customer hands you $1. How much change do you give?
A toy car costs $2.50. The customer pays with a $5 note. Count back the change.
Ring up three items: $1.20, 85¢, and $1.95. What is the total?
A $10 note covers a $6.85 order. How much change goes back to the customer?
